card.tag: The title is a grammar joke
card.title: Where 'Curiouser and curiouser!' comes from
card.moment: The episode borrows its title from the opening line of the second chapter of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, where Alice — suddenly growing — blurts it out.
card.idea: Lewis Carroll wrote the mistake on purpose. The proper comparative is 'more curious', and the narrator says so in the very next breath: Alice was so startled she momentarily forgot how to speak good English. The broken grammar is the character — she is too astonished to be correct.
card.why: A fitting title for an episode about Ted walking into a version of Richmond where nothing is arranged the way he left it. Being lost for the right words is the honest response to a world that has changed shape.
card.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, ch. II ('The Pool of Tears'), Lewis Carroll, 1865 — full text via Carnegie Mellon and USF's Lit2Go; episode details per Wikipedia.

card.title: The episode named for Alice introduces an Alice
card.moment: The same episode that lifts its title from Alice's most famous exclamation brings in Alice Chilton, the assistant coach who expected to get Ted's job.
card.idea: Nobody involved in the show has said this is deliberate, so treat it as something to notice rather than a confirmed joke. But the parallel does the work either way: the newcomer stumbling through a world he does not understand is Ted, and the person who actually belongs there is the one called Alice.
card.why: Small, and possibly a coincidence — worth knowing so you can decide for yourself on a rewatch.
card.source: Episode title and character per Wikipedia and TVLine; the Carroll line per the novel itself. Deliberate intent is not established by any source.

card.title: Curiosity has one author on this show
card.moment: Not on screen — in the credits. 'Curiouser and Curiouser!' is written by Leann Bowen, who also wrote season one's 'The Diamond Dogs'.
card.idea: 'The Diamond Dogs' is the darts episode — the one built entirely around being curious rather than judgmental. Six years and a whole new team later, the show hands its other curiosity episode to the same writer.
card.why: Television is written by committees and rooms, so a repeat like this is rarely an accident. If the season-one darts speech is the show's thesis, this is the same person picking the argument back up.
card.source: Writer and director credits per Wikipedia and The Movie Database for both episodes.

CORRECTED FROM THE CANDIDATE. The candidate cited a World Cup study as evidence women tear ACLs more often; that study (opened) reports 12.5% of women's players versus 7.7% of men's with a previous reconstruction but explicitly finds NO statistically significant difference (p = 0.34), so it is not used. The elevated-risk claim instead rests on FIFPRO's Project ACL (two to six times more likely; roughly two thirds non-contact) and Sky Sports reporting the UEFA elite club injury study at 64% non-contact. Alice's ACL history is corroborated by TVLine and Looper; Josie's torn ACL by the Forbes recap and the episode's Wikipedia plot summary. Sources conflict on Alice's former club (Arsenal academy vs Lewisham), so no club is named.

card.tag: The injury that runs the women's game
card.title: Why Alice knows exactly what Josie is facing
card.moment: Striker Josie tears her ACL in training and is gone for the season. Alice — until that moment the coldest person in the building — turns warm and steady, and goes with her.
card.idea: Alice's own playing career was ended by a run of ACL injuries. That is not a writer reaching for drama: the anterior cruciate ligament is the defining injury of women's football. FIFPRO puts the risk at somewhere between two and six times a man's, and roughly two thirds of the tears happen with nobody touching the player.
card.why: It reframes her whole introduction. The person who resents Ted most is also the only one in the room who has lived what just happened to Josie — and the show lets her be the one who handles it.
card.source: FIFPRO's Project ACL and Sky Sports on the UEFA elite club injury study; character detail via TVLine, Looper, Forbes and Wikipedia.

facts.verification_notes: The moment is corroborated by two opened recaps and the Wikipedia plot summary: Ted wins Alice over by showing he has learned her history rather than by arguing. The Simone Weil attribution — often floated loosely online — checks out: letter to Joe Bousquet, 13 April 1942, quoted in Simone Petrement's biography, and catalogued as such by WIST with agreement from Oxford Reference and Wikiquote.

card.title: He does not talk her round — he had already looked her up
card.moment: Alice has her resignation ready. Ted does not counter with optimism; he lays out what he has learned about her career and what ended it, and she stays.
card.idea: Simone Weil, in a 1942 letter: attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. Paying real attention costs something — time, effort, the willingness to be changed by what you find — which is why it lands as respect rather than flattery.
card.why: It is the season-one method without the season-one charm offensive. Ted cannot win this room by being likeable, so he wins one person by having bothered to learn her.
card.source: Weil to Joë Bousquet, 13 Apr 1942, cited in Simone Pétrement, Simone Weil: A Life (1976); scene per Forbes, Ready Steady Cut and Wikipedia.

Corroborated across four opened sources: Higgins' viability report concluding the women's team is unsustainable, the press ignoring them, the cramped quarters, Keeley engineering the switch to the visitors' room, and Rebecca backing the team anyway.

card.title: The opposition this season is a spreadsheet
card.moment: Higgins finishes his report and the answer is that the women's team does not add up. The cameras stay pointed at the men. The squad is crammed into a room that barely fits them, until Keeley engineers a swap for the visitors' dressing room and the players react to plumbing like it is a trophy.
card.idea: Ted Lasso has always needed someone to be wrong — Rupert, Nate, Ted's own avoidance. Here the obstacle has no face. It is what a club is willing to fund, and it does not care whether anyone believes.
card.why: It changes what a win looks like. You cannot out-kindness a balance sheet, so watch what Rebecca chooses to do with the numbers rather than about them.
card.groundingNotes: Corroborated across four opened sources: Higgins' viability report concluding the women's team is unsustainable, the press ignoring them, the cramped quarters, Keeley engineering the switch to the visitors' room, and Rebecca backing the team anyway.

One recap had suggested Beard took a role with the men's side; the Forbes recap and Ready Steady Cut agree, and Wikipedia is consistent with them, that Roy releases Beard from the men's team precisely so he can follow Ted to the women's staff. The dissenting summary appears to be an error.

card.title: Beard ends up back beside Ted, and Roy is why
card.moment: Beard is on Roy's staff and unsettled. Roy releases him — not as a rejection, but because he can see where Beard actually wants to be.
card.idea: Aristotle separates friendships of utility from friendships of virtue: one lasts as long as it is useful, the other because of who the other person is. Roy giving up a good coach he needs, to send him where he belongs, is the second kind — and it is Roy, of all people, doing it wordlessly.
card.why: Ted and Beard have been the show's steadiest pairing. Season four had to explain why they would be together again, and the answer turns out to be a favour from Roy rather than a contract.
card.source: Forbes and Ready Steady Cut recaps; Wikipedia. Aristotle's three friendships per Ted Lasso and Philosophy (Wiley, 2024).

card.title: The goalkeeper who wants to feel it
card.moment: Among the Lady Greyhounds is Katie, known as Boots, a keeper who will not wear gloves — she wants the sting of the ball in her hands on every save.
card.idea: The actor who plays her reads it as fear rather than toughness: someone frightened of being brilliant, holding herself back from the level she could reach. The refusal looks like intensity and is closer to self-sabotage.
card.why: One line of character detail that tells you what kind of squad this is, and plants something for the season to undo.
card.source: The Koalition breakdown; TVLine's interview with Jude Mack.

facts.verification_notes: Four opened sources converge on the same throughline: Ted cannot rerun the season-one playbook, arrives to scepticism rather than a squad ready to be charmed, and has to build for people whose circumstances are not the men's team's.

card.title: The playbook does not transfer
card.moment: Ted arrives with a reputation instead of anonymity, and a squad that has no reason to be charmed by him. Alice is the sharpest edge of that, but she is not the only one.
card.idea: Season one worked because nobody expected anything of him. That advantage is gone. What is left is the part that was never a trick — turning up, asking, and building for the people actually in front of you rather than the ones you succeeded with before.
card.why: It is the difference between a philosophy and a routine. If the biscuits and the signs were the method, they will fail here; if they were only ever the packaging, watch what he does instead.
card.source: Recaps at The Film Gordon, Seat42F, Ready Steady Cut and Forbes.
